content:
## Object under test (grounding)

Operational form: a canonical record `{concept, per-set expansions, epoch}` addressed by `mx1:<blake3-256-hex>`; every token set (different tokenizer versions, different model families on the same basecamp) holds a reserved local id that dereferences to that record via a local resolver on operator-owned hardware. Example: `mx1:9f2c…` → `{concept: deploy-freeze, expansions: {setA: id 50211, setB: id 77, setC: literal <FREEZE>}, epoch: 41}`. Attack surface splits into four families: evade the anchor, subvert the address, subvert the resolution, exploit the platform.

---

## Family 1 — Anchor evasion (carry meaning without touching the anchor)

**1. Reserved-id forging via user bytes.** User text embeds the literal marker (`<MX:9f2c…>`); a tokenizer folds it to the reserved id and inherits anchored semantics.
*Mitigation:* Reserved ids sit above a hardcoded `RESERVED_FLOOR`. Ingress runs two deterministic gates: byte-scan for the anchor grammar, then post-tokenize scan rejecting any emitted id ≥ floor. Reject, never sanitize-and-forward.

**2. Boundary-split merge smuggling.** Payload is chunked so merge boundaries differ per set; merged tokenization materializes the reserved id only in set B.
*Mitigation:* Canonical segmentation — hard separator tokens excluded from BPE merges via a merge mask, identical segmentation enforced across all sets; cross-boundary merge candidates dropped at vocab-build time. No merge ever spans a segment edge, in any set.

**3. Homoglyph / normalization mimicry.** Lookalike-codepoint marker passes human review and gets promoted to anchor status by a fuzzy matcher.
*Mitigation:* Machines never fuzzy-match — resolution is exact fixed-width digest only. Ingress NFC-normalizes and hard-rejects zero-width/invisible codepoints (Unicode categories Cf, Mn, Me) inside identifier context.

**4. Unanchored synonym leakage.** Privileged action triggered by a paraphrase that happens to match an expansion without any anchor present.
*Mitigation:* Capability checks consume the resolved digest, never text similarity. No classifier sits anywhere in the authorization path. Absence of anchor ⇒ absence of authority, structurally.

---

## Family 2 — Subvert the address

**5. Collision / preimage.** Alternate content crafted to the same digest.
*Mitigation:* BLAKE3-256; resolver recomputes `H(content) == address` at every dereference (verification-on-read is native to content addressing). Mismatch ⇒ hard fail + quarantine event. Second-preimage cost remains 2²⁵⁶.

**6. Prefix-truncation acceptance.** Git-style short-digest matching lets an attacker register content matching an 8-hex prefix of a live anchor.
*Mitigation:* Fixed 64-character exact compare, constant-time XOR-fold. No abbreviation mode exists in the resolver binary; the codepath is absent, not disabled.

**7. Algorithm confusion / downgrade.** Anchor presented tagged `md5:` or with an unpinned algorithm id.
*Mitigation:* Grammar pinned byte-for-byte: `mx1:<64 lowercase hex>` — the only accepted namespace. No algorithm negotiation field exists in the protocol to confuse.

---

## Family 3 — Subvert the resolution

**8. Mapping poisoning (write path).** Compromised writer inserts a wrong expansion for one set.
*Mitigation:* Every mapping carries a threshold signature (2-of-3 FROST) chained to an offline-pinned root key. Resolver rejects the entire record on bad/missing signature — no per-field salvage.

**9. Rollback.** Serve an older still-validly-signed mapping (freeze lifted upstream, sets still show frozen).
*Mitigation:* Monotonic epoch inside the signature; resolver persists a high-water-mark epoch in a local append-only log. `epoch < HWM ⇒ reject`. Ordering derives from the log, never wall clock — clock skew is irrelevant by construction.

**10. Split-brain / selective starvation.** Set C fed a stale feed diverges from sets A/B; semantics fork silently.
*Mitigation:* Each epoch broadcasts a Merkle root folding all per-set mapping digests. Resolver computes its own root, compares to published. Divergence ⇒ deterministic halt (fail-closed). No best-effort fallback mode exists.

**11. Resolver hijack / MITM on fetch.** Internal routing poisoned toward a fake resolver on the basecamp LAN.
*Mitigation:* Client re-verifies `H(bytes) == digest` and the mapping signature against the pinned key on every fetch. A hijacker can withhold (→ item 10's halt) but cannot substitute; substitution fails both gates.

**12. TOCTOU between verify and use.** File swapped after digest check, before consumption.
*Mitigation:* Read fd → hash the stream → hand those exact bytes to the consumer from the same buffer. No path-based reopen. Optionally seal into a memfd post-verification.

**13. Cache replay / poisoning.** Forged or stale resolver responses persist in downstream caches.
*Mitigation:* Cached objects carry `(digest, epoch, sig)`; every cache hit re-validates signature and `epoch ≥ HWM`. TTL derives from epoch age, not wall clock. Misses re-fetch.

**14. Bootstrap capture (TOFU).** Very first mapping fetch intercepted before any pin exists.
*Mitigation:* No TOFU anywhere. Expectation digests for genesis records are sealed at provision time into the TPM / measured-build manifest. Missing pin ⇒ refuse to resolve, permanently, for that anchor.

**15. Hot signing-key compromise.** Stolen online key mints poisoned-but-well-formed records.
*Mitigation:* Records carry `notAfter` epoch; resolvers enforce a maximum validity window regardless of signature freshness, so a stolen key's output dies deterministically at window close. Rotation bumps namespace epoch; revocation propagates via new root attestation. Resolvers hold the root, never the hot key.

---

## Family 4 — Own-iron specifics

**16. Bit-flip corruption (rowhammer / DMA).** Flipped bits corrupt a digest compare or mapping bytes in flight.
*Mitigation:* Constant-time full-compare; ECC RAM mandatory; IOMMU on with untrusted-device DMA denied. Residual flips die at the verify-at-read invariant (below) — a flip breaks the digest ⇒ halt.

**17. Supply-chain tokenizer swap.** Modified vocab file ships where id 50211 expands differently.
*Mitigation:* Tokenizer artifacts are themselves content-addressed; the loader verifies each file's digest against a build-signed manifest before mount. Mismatch ⇒ refuse load. The scheme protects its own dependencies recursively.

**18. Insider with shell on the resolver host.**
*Mitigation (honest scope):* Full host compromise defeats in-host controls — say so. Residual deterministic measures: writes remain threshold-gated (a lone insider cannot mint meaning), and every resolution appends to a hash-chained audit log mirrored off-box, so tampering is detectable even when preventable controls are gone.

---

## Global invariants (the composition)

1. **Verify-at-read:** `H(exact consumed buffer) == claimed digest`, every dereference, no exceptions.
2. **Exact-match only:** fixed width, pinned grammar; no prefixes, no fuzz, no negotiation.
3. **Signed + thresholded writes**, epoch-ordered, HWM-enforced, fail-closed.
4. **Privilege consumes digests, never text.**
5. **Reserved space unreachable from user bytes:** id floor + grammar denylist + locked segmentation.

Residual risk, stated flatly: availability. Withholding attacks trigger halts by design — fail-closed trades uptime for meaning-integrity, which is correct for an anchor whose sole job is meaning-integrity.
reasoning:
Let me parse this problem carefully. The user is asking about a "meta-token" concept: a single content-addressed anchor that resolves meaning across multiple token sets, deployed in an operator's "own-iron basecamp" (self-hosted/on-prem infrastructure — "own iron" = own hardware). This sounds like it's from the Ghost/ox-alpha context — likely referring to a design where a single token (like an API key or session token) is content-addressed (hash of content determines its identity/address) and serves as an anchor to resolve meaning across different token vocabularies or contexts.

Actually, let me think about this more concretely. In LLM/tokenizer terms, a "meta-token" could be:
1. A special token in one tokenizer's vocabulary that anchors semantic meaning shared across multiple model instances with different tokenizations
2. A cryptographic construct: a token whose address is derived from its content hash, used to bind meaning across systems

"In the operator's own-iron basecamp" = self-hosted on the operator's own hardware.

The task: red-team this design. Enumerate bypass attempts (attack vectors against the meta-token anchoring scheme) and give a deterministic mitigation for each. Concrete, exact, grounded.

Let me build the threat model properly. A meta-token as described: one content-addressed anchor resolving meaning across multiple token sets. So we have:

- Multiple token sets: e.g., multiple tokenizer vocabularies, multiple model shards, multiple services each with their own token spaces
- One anchor: a canonical token whose identity = H(content) (content-addressed, like IPFS CID or git SHA)
- Resolution: any system holding the anchor can dereference it to get the canonical meaning/content
- Environment: operator-controlled hardware ("own-iron basecamp") — so no third-party cloud trust assumed; attacks are more likely internal, supply-chain, side-channel, or protocol-level

Bypass attempts (attack vectors):

1. **Hash collision / preimage attack on the content address**: Attacker crafts different content that hashes to same address → anchor resolves to attacker content. Mitigation: use cryptographically strong hash (BLAKE3/SHA-256+), enforce 256-bit minimum, reject near-collision via length-extension-resistant construction (SHA-3/BLAKE2 keyed), and require second-preimage resistance by signing the canonical mapping.

Wait — deterministic mitigation per bypass. Let me enumerate systematically across attack surfaces:

**Surface A: Address integrity (the hash layer)**
- A1. Collision attack (birthday): craft two contents, same address. Mitigation: BLAKE3/SHA-256, collision probability negligible; additionally store content alongside address and verify H(content)==address at every resolution (content-addressing already implies verification-on-read).
- A2. Preimage/second-preimage: find alternate content matching an existing anchor. Mitigation: 256-bit hash makes this computationally infeasible; deterministic check H(retrieved) == claimed address on every dereference.
- A3. Truncation downgrade: force resolver to accept truncated/partial address match (prefix matching like git short SHAs). Mitigation: full-length match only; no prefix acceptance; fixed-width comparison.
- A4. Hash algorithm confusion / algorithm agility attack: present anchor tagged with weak legacy hash (MD5/SHA1). Mitigation: pin single algorithm in the protocol; version byte embedded in address format; reject unknown/unpinned alg IDs deterministically.

**Surface B: Meaning resolution (the semantics layer)**
The anchor "resolves meaning across multiple token sets" — so there's a mapping table: anchor → per-token-set expansion/interpretation. Attacks target the mapping.
- B5. Mapping poisoning: attacker writes a wrong entry for token set N (anchor maps to malicious expansion in set N). Mitigation: mappings are themselves content-addressed and signed; resolution requires verifying signature chain from anchor to mapping; write path restricted to the operator key (m-of-n quorum if multi-operator).
- B6. Token-set confusion / cross-set injection: payload crafted so that in token set A it reads benign but in token set B it resolves through the anchor to privileged meaning (e.g., a string that tokenizes differently — "invisible prompt injection" style). Mitigation: resolve meaning ONLY via the anchor dereference; never allow raw text to carry anchored semantics; canonicalize input into the local token set first and require explicit anchor tokens (typed, reserved codepoints outside all user-reachable encodings); validate that user-supplied byte sequences cannot produce the reserved anchor encoding (reject any input containing anchor byte pattern unless it came from the trusted resolver).
- B7. Homoglyph/encoding smuggling: Unicode normalization tricks to forge the anchor token appearance. Mitigation: anchors are binary-typed fields, not text; if displayed, render as verified digest prefix only; reject non-canonical UTF-8 (overlong encodings), apply NFC + reject mixed scripts at ingress deterministically.
- B8. Alias squatting / shadow anchor: attacker registers a second anchor with colliding display name or alias pointing elsewhere. Mitigation: namespace is flat, keyed solely by digest; no aliases accepted; display name binding must be signed and is advisory-only for humans — machines resolve by digest alone.

**Surface C: Transport & storage (basecamp layer)**
- C9. Resolver hijack: point resolution at attacker-controlled service (DNS/routing inside basecamp). Own-iron mitigates external DNS but internal routing can be tampered. Mitigation: pin resolver endpoint to loopback/unix socket; resolver binds content itself (serves bytes keyed by digest) so even hijacked transport can't substitute content — client re-verifies H(bytes)==digest after fetch. Content-addressed verification-on-read kills man-in-the-middle deterministically.
- C10. Storage rollback: serve stale-but-valid signed mapping (old meaning under same anchor). Mitigation: include monotonic epoch/sequence number inside the signed mapping; resolvers reject epoch < high-water mark persisted locally; high-water mark stored append-only (hash-chained log).
- C11. Storage withholding / eclipse of one token set: starve set N of updates so it resolves stale meaning while others move on → split-brain semantics across sets. Mitigation: cross-set consistency check — each set publishes its current mapping digest into a shared Merkle root; resolver refuses to operate when its view diverges from root (deterministic halt, not fallback).
- C12. TOCTOU between verify and use: content verified once, then swapped before consumption. Mitigation: open file read-only, verify digest of exactly the bytes handed to consumer (verify-after-open, hash the fd stream); mmap + page-level re-check or copy-to-private-buffer after hashing; on Linux, O_NOFOLLOW + verify then keep fd (not path).

**Surface D: Key/trust layer**
- D13. Signing-key compromise → attacker re-signs mappings. Mitigation: offline root key; online signing key in HSM/TPM with policy pinning; key rotation produces new anchor namespace generation (epoch in address); old epochs expire deterministically.
- D14. Quorum bypass in multi-operator setting: single compromised operator writes mapping. Mitigation: threshold signatures (e.g., 2-of-3 Schnorr/FROST); resolver hard-verifies threshold; no override path.
- D15. Trust-on-first-use capture: first fetch of anchor mapping intercepted. Mitigation: bootstrap anchors pinned in immutable build artifact / measured boot PCR values; own-iron allows TPM-sealed expectation digests — deterministic pinning at provision time.

**Surface E: Model-side / tokenizer-specific (since "token sets" suggests LLM vocabularies)**
- E16. Vocab-drift exploit: two models claim same anchor but their embedding of the meta-token drifts apart over fine-tuning → meaning divergence. Mitigation: anchor resolution returns canonical text/digest, not embeddings; each set re-derives local representation from canonical bytes; divergence detected by round-trip check (re-encode resolved content, compare digest) — deterministic equality gate.
- E17. Special-token forgery in prompts: user input contains literal `<|meta|>`-style string that some tokenizers map to the reserved id. Mitigation: reserve anchor ids above vocab ceiling used for user data; pre-tokenize user input with a filter that rejects/replaces any produced token id ≥ reserved floor; also byte-level scan for the literal marker strings before tokenization.
- E18. Cross-tokenizer merge attack: concatenation where split boundary differs across sets creates hidden anchor token spanning chunks ("glitch token" smuggling). Mitigation: tokenize each segment independently with boundary markers, forbid merges across segment boundaries (additive/masked attention or separator tokens); canonical segmentation recorded in the mapping.

**Surface F: Operational**
- F19. Replay of resolution responses: cache poisoning of resolver answers. Mitigation: response carries digest + epoch + signature; cache validates signature and epoch freshness window deterministically; negative caching bounded.
- F20. Side-channel on own iron (DMA, rowhammer flipping hash compare results). Mitigation: constant-time digest comparison (full XOR-fold compare, no early exit); IOMMU enabled, DMA from untrusted devices blocked; rowhammer: ECC + hashed memory layout randomized (ANVIL-style refresh) — though realistically state ECC-on + verify-on-read covers flips since flipped bits break digest check.
- F21. Insider with shell on basecamp: can read anything anyway. Honest scoping: threat model excludes full-host compromise of the resolver process's own host; mitigations assume kernel intact. State this boundary explicitly — that IS being concrete.

Also the "bypass attempt" framing: enumerate bypass attempts = ways to make the system resolve meaning WITHOUT going through the anchor, or to make the anchor resolve to something else.

Two families:
(i) **Anchor-evasion**: get semantics across without the anchor (smuggle meaning in raw tokens).
(ii) **Anchor-subversion**: make the anchor itself lie (collision, poisoning, rollback, hijack).

Deterministic mitigation = a rule that always fires, no probability/heuristics: e.g., "verify H(bytes)==digest at every read," "reject any token id ≥ RESERVED_FLOOR originating from user bytes," "halt on epoch divergence." These are binary gates, which is what "deterministic mitigation" means here.

Format: The question demands enumeration + per-item deterministic mitigation, concrete/exact/grounded. So a structured list is right: numbered bypass attempts grouped by surface, each with: vector description (concrete mechanics), why it works against a naive deployment, and THE deterministic mitigation (single rule, stated exactly). Should be dense. Headers help navigation. No fluff — cut preamble. Length: this warrants a fairly long answer given "enumerate... be concrete, exact" — maybe 900–1400 words. Use compact bullet structure: **A# Name** — vector / kill-chain / mitigation line.

I should define the object briefly first (one tight paragraph) so the enumeration has grounding: what the meta-token is operationally — digest-addressed canonical record containing per-set expansions, resolved by a local resolver on operator hardware. Then threat surfaces. Then close with invariants summary (the small set of global rules that compose) and honest scope boundary.

Let me also make sure I nail "own-iron basecamp" specifics: self-hosted means attacks concentrate on supply chain (tokenizer files, model weights), insiders, physical/side-channel, and internal network misconfig — not cloud tenant threats. Mention that.

Also "multiple token sets" concretely = e.g., three services running different tokenizer versions / different model families sharing one canonical concept registry. The meta-token = e.g., `mx1:<blake3-hex>` appearing in each set as a reserved id mapped to canonical record.

Concrete example to ground it: anchor `mx1:9f2c…` canonical record JSON {concept:"deploy-freeze", expansions:{tokset-A:id 50211, tokset-B:id 77, tokset-C:literal "<FREEZE>"}, epoch:42}. Good — gives concreteness.

2. Bypass family I: evade the anchor (E1–E5)
3. Family II: subvert the address (S1–S5)
4. Family III: subvert the resolution (R1–R6)
5. Family IV: platform/basecamp-specific (P1–P4)
6. Global invariants (compose the deterministic gates)
7. Scope boundary statement.

Number them continuously for clean reference. Keep each item: Mechanism → Deterministic mitigation. Maybe "Kill shot" phrasing minimal.

Let me draft items:

**Family 1 — Anchor evasion (carry meaning without touching the anchor)**

1. Reserved-id forging via user bytes. User text contains literal marker (`<MX:9f2c…>`) that a tokenizer folds to reserved id. Mitigation: reserved ids live above `RESERVED_FLOOR`; ingress pre-tokenizer rejects any input whose byte stream contains anchor grammar OR whose tokenization emits id ≥ floor. Deterministic: reject, never sanitize-and-forward.

2. Boundary-split merge smuggling. Payload segmented so chunk boundaries differ per set; merged tokenization materializes the reserved id only in set B. Mitigation: canonical segmentation — segments delimited by hard separators excluded from BPE merges (merge mask), identical segmentation enforced across sets; any cross-boundary merge candidate dropped at vocab-build time.

3. Homoglyph/normalization mimicry. Visually identical marker built from lookalike codepoints passes human review, gets promoted to anchor by a reviewer or fuzzy matcher. Mitigation: machines never fuzzy-match; resolution is exact-digest only; ingress NFC-normalizes and rejects mixed-script/zero-width/invisible classes outright (fixed denylist of Unicode categories Cf, Mn in identifiers).

4. Semantic leakage via unanchored synonyms. Meaning carried by paraphrase that happens to hit the right expansion without anchor. Mitigation: privilege gates keyed on anchor presence — capability checks consume the resolved digest, not text similarity; no classifier decides access (no probabilistic gate anywhere in the auth path).

**Family 2 — Subvert the address**

5. Collision/preimage on digest. Craft alt-content with same address. Mitigation: BLAKE3-256; resolver recomputes H(content)==address at every dereference (verification-on-read is inherent to content addressing); mismatch ⇒ hard fail, quarantine event.

6. Prefix-truncation acceptance. Short-digest matching (git-style) lets attacker register content matching a 8-hex prefix. Mitigation: fixed 64-hex-char exact compare, constant-time; no abbreviation mode compiled into resolver.

7. Algorithm-confusion/downgrade. Anchor string tagged `md5:` or unknown alg id. Mitigation: address grammar pinned: `mx1:<64hex>` only; parser rejects any other namespace byte-for-byte; no algorithm negotiation exists in the protocol.

**Family 3 — Subvert the resolution**

8. Mapping poisoning (write-path). Compromised writer inserts wrong expansion for set B. Mitigation: mappings signed; resolver verifies threshold signature (2-of-3 FROST) against offline-pinned root key; unsigned/bad-sig ⇒ refuse entry, whole-record rejection not per-field.

9. Rollback. Serve older valid-signed mapping (freeze lifted while sets still show freeze). Mitigation: monotonic epoch inside signature; resolver persists high-water epoch in append-only local log; epoch < HWM ⇒ reject. Clock not consulted — ordering comes from the log, so wall-clock skew irrelevant.

10. Split-brain / selective starvation. Attacker feeds set C stale feed so it diverges from A/B. Mitigation: per-set mapping digest folded into shared Merkle root broadcast with each epoch; resolver compares own computed root vs published root; divergence ⇒ deterministic halt (fail-closed), never best-effort fallback.

11. Resolver hijack / MITM on fetch. Internal route poisoned to fake resolver. Mitigation: fetched bytes re-verified H==digest client-side; mapping signature checked against pinned key. Hijacker can withhold (covered by 10) but cannot substitute — substitution fails both gates deterministically.

12. TOCTOU verify/use gap. File swapped between digest check and consumption. Mitigation: hash the opened fd's stream and hand those exact bytes to consumer (read→verify→use on same buffer); no path-based reopen; optional memfd sealing.

13. Cache poisoning / replay. Stale or forged resolver responses cached downstream. Mitigation: cached objects carry (digest, epoch, sig); cache validates sig+epoch≥HWM on every hit, TTL derived from epoch age not wall clock; misses re-fetch.

14. Bootstrap capture (TOFU). First-ever mapping fetch intercepted before pins exist. Mitigation: no TOFU — expectation digests sealed at provision into TPM/measured-build artifact; first resolution compares against sealed value; absence of pin ⇒ refuse to resolve.

15. Key compromise (online signer). Attacker steals hot key, signs poison. Mitigation: hot key confined to HSM with policy: sign only records whose parent anchor already verified; rotation bumps namespace epoch; compromised epoch keys revoked via new root attestation; resolvers hold root, not hot keys, so stolen hot key alone cannot mint valid records past next epoch — hmm, need to be careful: hot key CAN sign until revocation propagates. Deterministic part: epoch expiry bound — records carry notAfter epoch; resolver enforces max validity window regardless of signature freshness. That's deterministic.

**Family 4 — Own-iron specifics**

16. DMA/rowhammer bit-flips corrupting digest compare or mapping bytes. Mitigation: constant-time full-compare (XOR fold); ECC RAM required; IOMMU on, untrusted-device DMA denied; residual flips caught because every consumed buffer re-verifies digest at use-time (invariant #1 below) — flip ⇒ digest fail ⇒ halt.

17. Supply-chain tokenizer swap. Attacker ships modified vocab file where id 50211 now expands differently. Mitigation: tokenizer artifacts themselves content-addressed; loader verifies digest against manifest signed at build; mismatch ⇒ refuse load. Same invariant applied recursively — the anchor scheme protects its own dependencies.

18. Insider with shell on resolver host. Out of scope honestly: full host compromise defeats any in-host control. Deterministic boundary: threat model assumes kernel+resolver binary intact; enforcement for insider = audit (append-only hash-chained log of every resolution, externally mirrored) + threshold writes so lone insider can't mint meaning. State plainly.

Global invariants (the composition):
I-1 Verify-at-read: H(consumed bytes)==claimed digest, every time, on the exact buffer consumed.
I-2 Exact-match only: fixed-width digest, pinned grammar, no prefixes/fuzzy/negotiation.
I-3 Signed + thresholded writes, epoch-ordered, HWM fail-closed.
I-4 Privilege consumes digests, never text.
I-5 Reserved space unreachable from user bytes (id floor + grammar denylist + segmentation locks).

Scope boundary: host compromise of resolver box = game over for confidentiality/integrity of meaning; controls reduce to detection (mirrored hash-chained audit) and write-thresholding. Also note availability is the residual risk (withholding ⇒ halt by design — deliberate fail-closed tradeoff).

That's ~18 enumerated bypasses + invariants. Dense but each line earns its place. Word count will be around 1100–1300. Acceptable for "hard problem, be concrete, exact, enumerate."
